newsitem.title: UK: Precious Metals Outlook -- PGM tensions continue.
newsitem.headline: Precious Metals Outlook -- PGM tensions continue.

text.p: Tensions in the platinum and palladium metals (PGMs) markets look like continuing at least through this month or until clear evidence emerges that Russia has begun its long delayed 1997 export campaign, dealers said.
The price of platinum reached its highest level since 1990 on Friday and palladium by far the scarcer of the two currently was at levels not seen since 1980 most of last week.

Platinum rose $100 per ounce last week to $500 on Friday. Palladium prices have doubled this year to around $240.00 They were indicated at $475/$485 and $230.00/$240.00 respectively on Monday morning.

There are no serious signs of the prices reversing near-term -- or of more material coming on to the market, although one market analyst said small parcels of material were being offered to industrial users by a holder of metal seeking to cash in without affecting the price on the dealer market.
The delay in Russia starting its 1997 export campaign is propping up the prices. Russia is the world's leading palladium exporter and second biggest platinum supplier.
"There is not much likelihood of things changing until Russia starts to deliver," a dealer said.

Russia supplies 60 percent of world palladium and about 20 percent of platinum, but fiscal and administrative problems and a possible change of marketing strategy led to a suspension of exports last December.

German catalytic converter maker Degussa AG could face production curbs if the current supply squeeze on the platinum market continues for another three to four weeks, a company official said on Friday.
"That is the warning flag we are raising," Ralf Drieselmann, head of precious metals trading, told Reuters.
Degussa produces 15 to 25 percent of the world's catalytic converters, which filter harmful gases from auto exhausts.
Market stresses reached boiling point late last week.

The London Platinum and Palladium Market Association (LPPMA) met last Thursday to review conditions amid talk of defaults and mounting losses and calls for legal action against speculative investment funds allegedly "cornering" the market.
"The members confirmed that there were no defaults in the market," said Trevor Pitts, chairman of the LPPMA after the meeting.
Rumours of the possibility of a default on delivery had been the hard pressed markets' latest scare.
Significantly Pitts stated, "The key issue really depends on when the Russians begin exporting again."
Dealers conceded that unless liquidity returned to the market, a default in delivery against contract could not be ruled out as long as the tense situation remained.
"The problem was nobody had the stuff to lend and when some people detected this they insisted on delivery of the physical metal, not cash," a senior dealer said.

The market is self-regulated by the LPPMA since the two metals are not traded on an exchange, British official regulatory officials said. The Bank of England has no oversight over them, a Bank spokeswoman said.

Lack of Russian supplies has been compounded by speculative buying by investment funds. The U.S. Tiger Management Fund is said to be holding 1.5 million ounces of palladium, roughly 20 percent of 1996 world demand.

Funds are reluctant to open the floodgates since each time they dribble out small parcels of the metal, prices start to crumble, one dealer said. "The funds have to play this very delicately if they are to have a profitable position," he said.
Trading in these metals has always been a low key business compared to that in gold.

They only became "official" markets in London in 1989, which was 70 years after the gold market established its price "fixing" process which provides a twice-daily reference point on which pricing for contracts can be based.

Prices of the rare white metals soared at the end of the 1970s, when gold and silver reached historic highs on fears of inflation, after the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries lifted the cost of oil to $40 a barrel.
Platinum reached its highest unofficial value at around $1,050 in early March 1980 and palladium peaked at around $335.00.

Since the official fixings began, palladium's top price was $181.50 in 1989 when laboratory tests suggested that "cold fusion" might work, creating a new demand for the metal. But the price collapsed when further research failed to support initial results.

Demand for both metals and especially palladium has boomed in the past 10 years as governments have legislated to clean up car exhaust fumes and the electronics industry has advanced making increasing use of their high conductivity properties.

Palladium demand has trebled and Russian exports had risen to a record 4.6 million ounces last year mainly from government stockpiles from 1.70 million ounces in 1987, according to statistics from the world's leading platinum group metals refiner Johnson Matthey.
